all.limitation: MVFA's zero-shot setting requires supervised medical-source adaptation and evaluates transfer to a held-out target domain, rather than medical anomaly detection without medical labels.
all.explanation: Annotated medical data are used to construct the medically adapted model before zero-shot testing. Consequently, zero-shot here describes the target scenario, not annotation-free medical adaptation. The benchmark also contains two retinal-OCT datasets, so dataset holdout and modality/anatomy holdout are not interchangeable descriptions; this does not establish that either OCT dataset actually trained the other.

evidence.quote: This adaptation utilizes a medical training dataset $\mathcal{D}_{med}$, which consists of annotated samples from the medical field, enabling the transformation of $\mathcal{M}_{nat}$ into $\mathcal{M}_{med}$.

Here, $\mathcal{D}_{med}$ is a pre-training dataset that is composed of medical data from different modalities and anatomical regions than those in the test samples, which assesses the model's generalization to unseen scenarios.
In this configuration, a designated target dataset was chosen for testing, while the remaining datasets with different modalities and anatomical regions were employed for training.
The benchmark includes two different OCT AD datasets.

all.suggested_fix: Run explicitly grouped modality/anatomy holdouts, jointly excluding RESC and OCT17 for retinal-OCT testing, and publish the source-dataset membership and source image/mask budgets for each target.
all.verdict_reason: The authors explicitly define zero-shot relative to a held-out target while requiring annotated medical-source adaptation, and the two OCT datasets alone do not establish cross-training.

all.limitation: MVFA's comparisons with normal-only baselines change anomaly-label supervision as well as the training-data regime, rather than comparing methods under a common supervision condition.
all.explanation: The authors explicitly attribute MVFA's advantage over CLIP and WinCLIP to using a few abnormal samples. They also state that the all-normal training sets contain considerably more images than the few-shot sets. These results compare different supervision regimes, whereas the supervised April-GAN comparison provides a more directly relevant control for the proposed adaptation.

evidence.quote: MVFA's advantage lies in its ability to effectively utilize a few abnormal samples, leading to significant gains over these methods.
It is important to highlight that this ``all-normal'' training set encompasses considerably more data compared to the limited data used in the few-shot scenario.
Building upon WinCLIP, April-GAN~ maps visual features extracted from CLIP to the linear space where the text features are located, supervised by pixel-level annotated data.

all.suggested_fix: Run a fixed-K normal-only versus mixed normal/abnormal MVFA supervision ablation, documenting support identities, class/mask counts, source-training counts and normal-bank size, with April-GAN receiving matched supervised supports.
all.verdict_reason: The authors explicitly distinguish the training regimes and attribute MVFA's advantage over normal-only methods to abnormal supervision, confirming that these comparisons are not supervision-matched.

all.limitation: Anomaly-segmentation evidence and BGAD comparisons are restricted to BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC, while OCT17, ChestXray and HIS contribute classification-only evidence.
all.explanation: This limits demonstrated segmentation generality to the three mask-annotated datasets. OCT17 and RESC are both retinal OCT, so OCT17's classification-only status means missing additional segmentation evidence within that modality, not another untested modality. Although the setup describes BGAD as segmentation-only, the authors also report its classification comparison on pixel-annotated datasets; the restriction concerns annotation availability and comparison coverage, not complete absence of BGAD classification results.

evidence.quote: Among these, BrainMRI~, LiverCT~, and RESC~ datasets are used for both anomaly classification (AC) and segmentation (AS), while OCT17~, ChestXray~, and HIS~ are solely for AC.
We evaluate these methods for AC and AS, excluding BGAD, which is exclusively applied for segmentation due to its requirement for pixel-level annotations during training.
Compared to BGAD~, MVFA shows an average improvement of 9.18\% in AUC for AC and 3.53\% in AUC for AS, in datasets with pixel-level annotations.

The RESC dataset~ offers pixel-level segmentation labels, delineating regions affected by retinal edema. In contrast, the OCT17 dataset~ primarily serves for classification tasks, featuring retinal OCT images categorized into three types of anomalies.

all.suggested_fix: Add mask-annotated support and test subsets for OCT17, ChestXray and HIS, compare MVFA and BGAD on identical supports, and report separate image/mask budgets and segmentation-loss handling for image-only samples.
all.verdict_reason: The authors explicitly restrict AS to BrainMRI, LiverCT, and RESC, and BGAD's reported results cover those datasets while also including AC scores.

all.limitation: The paper quantifies both medical classification and segmentation performance using ROC AUC, restricting the reported gains to image-level and pixel-level discrimination scores.
all.explanation: The evaluation protocol explicitly defines image-level AUC for classification and pixel-level AUC for segmentation. Consequently, the reported improvements quantify these metrics and cannot be recast as numerical improvements in lesion overlap or clinical sensitivity at a particular specificity.

evidence.quote: The area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve metric (AUC) is used to quantify the performance.
This metric is a standard in AD evaluation, with separate considerations for image-level AUC in AC and pixel-level AUC in AS.

all.suggested_fix: Re-score the existing test predictions with Dice/IoU where masks are available, lesion-level FROC, precision–recall metrics and calibration, counting any target-domain threshold-selection labels within the few-shot budget.
all.verdict_reason: Only image-level and pixel-level ROC AUC improvements are quantified, but the authors do not explicitly discuss the resulting lack of overlap or clinical operating-point evidence as a limitation.

all.limitation: The MRI/CT and histopathology evaluations use selected 2D slices and extracted patches, rather than complete-volume or whole-slide predictions.
all.explanation: BrainMRI selects FLAIR slices within depths 60–100, LiverCT uses 2D axial slices, and HIS testing uses patches extracted from testing whole slides. The reported results therefore establish performance on those extracted units rather than complete-volume or whole-slide decisions. This is a task-granularity qualification, not an assertion of patient- or slide-level leakage.

evidence.quote: To account for variations in brain images at different depths, slices within the depth range of 60 to 100 of the 3D FLAIR volumes are selected.
Each extracted 2D slice was saved in PNG format and has an image size of $240\times 240$ pixels.
The scans are then cropped into 2D axial slices, containing 1,452 2D slices for training and 1,493 2D slices for testing.
For testing, 1,003 normal and 997 abnormal patches from the 115 testing WSIs are utilized.

all.suggested_fix: Evaluate an explicit slice-/patch-aggregation variant on patient-/volume-/slide-disjoint complete MRI/CT studies and HIS whole slides, reporting case-level performance alongside the existing 2D scores.
all.verdict_reason: The dataset descriptions confirm selected MRI slices, axial CT slices, and histopathology patches, while the limitation on complete-volume or whole-slide conclusions is inferred rather than explicitly acknowledged.

all.limitation: MVFA's lightweight adaptation retains the full 24-layer CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder and adds multi-level nearest-neighbor memory-bank comparisons during few-shot inference.
all.explanation: The method adds small bottleneck layers while leaving the pretrained backbone unchanged. Its few-shot branch also compares test features against normal memory-bank features at each level. Thus, lightweight describes adapter-based tuning, not replacement of the encoder or a memory-free inference pipeline.

evidence.quote: This method appends a small set of learnable bottleneck linear layers to the visual branches of CLIP while keeping its original backbone unchanged, thus enabling adaptation at multiple feature levels.
We utilize the CLIP with ViT-L/14 architecture, with input images at a resolution of 240. The model comprises a total of 24 layers, which are divided into 4 stages, each encompassing 6 layers.

The few-shot AC and AS scores, denoted as $c_{few}$ and $\mathcal{S}_{few}$, are derived from the minimum distance between the test feature and the memory bank features at each level, through a nearest neighbor search process,

all.suggested_fix: Benchmark zero-shot-only, few-shot-only and combined inference over increasing normal-bank sizes, reporting total/trainable parameters, per-image latency, peak memory and AUC on the reported GPU.
all.verdict_reason: The full frozen 24-layer encoder and multi-level normal-memory searches are explicitly described, but distinguishing lightweight tuning from lightweight inference is the extractor's interpretation.

all.limitation: At K=4, the multi-level ensemble's reported average gain over Layer 2 is only 0.13 AUC points for classification and 0.05 for segmentation.
all.explanation: Layer 2 achieves 88.84%/98.62% classification/segmentation AUC, compared with 88.97%/98.67% for the ensemble. The benefit over the strongest individual layer is therefore incremental in this averaged K=4 experiment. This is a magnitude caveat, not a claim that either architecture is statistically inferior.

evidence.quote: The results presented in Table~ demonstrate that among individual layers, Layer 2 yielded the highest performance, achieving 88.84\% in AC and 98.62\% in AS.
However, the ensemble method, which integrates features from all layers, outperformed single-layer approaches, recording AUCs of 88.97\% in AC and 98.67\% in AS.
The average AUCs (in \%) of all six datasets for AC and AS under the few-shot setting (K=4) are reported.

all.suggested_fix: Repeat Layer-2-versus-ensemble testing on identical K=4 supports across random draws, report paired patient-/volume-/slide-clustered confidence intervals, and count any layer-selection labels within K.
all.verdict_reason: The reported K=4 ensemble and Layer 2 averages differ by exactly 0.13 AC and 0.05 AS AUC points, although the authors present this as an improvement rather than a marginal-gain caveat.

all.limitation: The supplementary results contain numerical regressions under multi-level training, including ChestXray Layer 3 classification AUC decreasing from 79.75% to 58.32%.
all.explanation: The main text's consistency statement concerns layer averages across datasets. The supplementary per-dataset tables nevertheless contain a lower ChestXray result for this layer under multi-level training. Consequently, consistency across layer averages should not be interpreted as improvement in every dataset–layer combination.

evidence.quote: Moreover, multi-level training consistently exceeds the performance of single-layer training, reinforcing the benefits of our multi-level adaptation approach across all layers.
Ablation study of multi-level features without multi-level training.
Ablation study of multi-level features with multi-level training.

all.suggested_fix: Repeat matched K=4 ChestXray experiments comparing single-layer training, uniform multi-level losses and adaptive loss balancing, reporting paired confidence intervals and counting model-selection labels within K.
all.verdict_reason: The supplementary tables directly show ChestXray Layer 3 AC falling from 79.75% to 58.32%, a dataset-specific regression the authors do not explicitly discuss.

all.limitation: In the reported zero-shot BrainMRI test, MVFA's segmentation AUC of 90.27% is below April-GAN's 91.79%.
all.explanation: The average zero-shot segmentation improvement over April-GAN coexists with a 1.52-percentage-point numerical disadvantage on BrainMRI. This qualifies the cross-domain segmentation advantage at an individual target domain rather than contradicting the reported aggregate improvement.

evidence.quote: Similarly, against April-GAN~, MVFA achieves an average AUC improvement of 6.24\% for AC and 2.03\% for AS across all datasets, underscoring its effectiveness in the challenging zero-shot medical AD setting.

all.suggested_fix: Repeat the BrainMRI holdout with matched source annotation budgets for MVFA and April-GAN, reporting volume-clustered uncertainty and lesion-size-stratified pixel AUC and Dice.
all.verdict_reason: The zero-shot table reports BrainMRI AS AUC of 90.27% for MVFA versus 91.79% for April-GAN, but the authors discuss the aggregate improvement rather than this exception.

all.limitation: The few-shot tables show exceptions to MVFA's numerical superiority: April-GAN has higher OCT17 classification AUC at all four shot counts, and BGAD has higher LiverCT segmentation AUC at K=2.
all.explanation: The OCT17 comparisons favor April-GAN at K=2,4,8,16 despite MVFA's stronger aggregate performance. At K=2, LiverCT segmentation AUC is 98.71% for BGAD versus 96.57% for MVFA. These dataset/task/shot-specific exceptions qualify uniform superiority, not the authors' average improvement claims.
all.suggested_fix: Repeat MVFA–April-GAN comparisons on OCT17 and MVFA–BGAD comparisons on LiverCT over matched K-shot draws, report patient-/volume-clustered intervals, and include any model-selection annotations in K.
all.verdict_reason: The few-shot tables favor April-GAN on OCT17 AC at every reported K and BGAD on LiverCT AS at K=2, without an explicit author discussion of these exceptions.

all.limitation: On ChestXray at K=4, MVFA's 81.95% AUC is below MedCLIP's 84.06%, a comparison the authors qualify by attributing MedCLIP's advantage to overlapping ChestXray pretraining.
all.explanation: The authors explicitly acknowledge the ChestXray exception and attribute it to overlapping pretraining data. Prior target-domain exposure is therefore a stated caveat in interpreting this comparison. The exception limits any claim of best performance on every dataset without negating the reported mean improvements.

evidence.quote: While MedCLIP~ shows superior results on ChestXray because it was trained on large-scale overlapping ChestXray data in our medical AD benchmark, it lacks broad generalization capabilities, as evidenced by its performance on other datasets.
MedCLIP~ & EMNLP 2022 & 75.89 & 84.06

all.suggested_fix: Audit image-/patient-level overlap between MedCLIP pretraining and the ChestXray test set, then report AUC stratified by confirmed overlap, confirmed non-overlap and unknown exposure.
all.verdict_reason: The K=4 table confirms 81.95% versus 84.06% ChestXray AUC, and the authors explicitly acknowledge MedCLIP's advantage and attribute it to overlapping pretraining data.

all.limitation: The dual-adapter architecture's reported K=4 classification improvement does not extend to OCT17, where its AUC is 99.38% versus 99.87% for the single adapter.
all.explanation: The authors appropriately qualify the dual adapter's advantage as applying to almost all datasets. Its average classification improvement coexists with this OCT17 exception. The 0.49-percentage-point difference near the AUC ceiling is a numerical exception, not by itself an established reliable architectural disadvantage.

evidence.quote: According to the results in Table~, the dual-adapter approach outperforms the single-adapter model on almost all the datasets.

all.suggested_fix: Repeat the single-/dual-adapter comparison on identical K=4 OCT17 supports across random draws, report paired patient-clustered confidence intervals, and count architecture-selection labels within K.
all.verdict_reason: The authors qualify dual-adapter superiority as applying to almost all datasets, and their table identifies OCT17 as the exception at 99.38% versus 99.87% AC AUC.

all.limitation: MVFA's MVTec segmentation results are not uniformly superior, with only a 0.05-point average AUC gain over WinCLIP and lower AUCs on cable and transistor.
all.explanation: The main text describes industrial performance as comparable. Average segmentation AUC is 96.32% for MVFA versus 96.27% for WinCLIP, while the supplementary results show cable at 87.3% versus 94.9% and transistor at 80.9% versus 88.5%. These exceptions qualify the supplementary statement of significant outperformance. They concern the industrial evaluation, not the paper's central medical-transfer objective.

evidence.quote: As shown in Table~, although our main focus is not in-domain scenarios, MVFA shows comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods in a few-shot setting (K=4).
MVFA significantly outperforms competing methods, highlighting its superior generalization capabilities.

all.suggested_fix: Repeat paired MVTec comparisons on shared K=4 supports and report category-specific and average effect sizes with confidence intervals, separately from the medical-transfer claims.
all.verdict_reason: The main text explicitly calls MVTec performance comparable, and the tables substantiate the 0.05-point average AS advantage and lower cable and transistor results.

all.limitation: The dataset-level leave-one-out protocol does not clearly establish whether both retinal OCT datasets are excluded when claiming unseen-modality and unseen-anatomy generalization.
all.explanation: RESC and OCT17 share retinal anatomy and OCT modality, while evaluation is described as leaving out one target dataset. Although the text says training uses different modalities, it does not provide per-fold dataset lists confirming joint exclusion; retaining the companion OCT dataset would make these results within-modality, within-anatomy transfer.

evidence.quote: In this configuration, a designated target dataset was chosen for testing, while the remaining datasets with different modalities and anatomical regions were employed for training.
Retinal OCT: The benchmark includes two different OCT AD datasets.

all.suggested_fix: Jointly hold out RESC and OCT17 as one retinal-OCT domain, publish every fold's training datasets, and compare against the dataset-level holdout results.
all.verdict_reason: The paper identifies two retinal OCT datasets but provides no explicit fold memberships confirming that both are excluded from training in either retinal target fold.

all.limitation: BrainMRI converts volumes into multiple slices without documenting patient-disjoint training, testing, and few-shot sampling, leaving independence unverified.
all.explanation: Neighboring slices from one FLAIR volume can share substantial anatomical and acquisition information, but the reported protocol does not specify patient or volume allocation. If patients overlap across splits, performance could be inflated; even with disjoint patients, correlated slice observations do not constitute independent patient-level evidence.

evidence.quote: To account for variations in brain images at different depths, slices within the depth range of 60 to 100 of the 3D FLAIR volumes are selected.
Each extracted 2D slice was saved in PNG format and has an image size of $240\times 240$ pixels.

all.suggested_fix: Partition patients before extracting slices, draw few-shot examples from distinct training patients, and evaluate with patient-clustered confidence intervals.
all.verdict_reason: BrainMRI extraction and image counts are described without patient- or volume-disjoint training, testing, and support-sampling rules, leaving independence undocumented rather than demonstrating leakage.

all.limitation: LiverCT lacks a source-matched normal-training control, leaving lesion-detection performance entangled with BTCV-to-LiTS acquisition and population shift.
all.explanation: Normal-only baselines learn from BTCV, whereas test scans come from LiTS, so source differences can distort anomaly scores independently of lesions. This is a legitimate transfer challenge, but without a within-LiTS normal-training control, weak baseline results cannot be separated from mismatch to the learned normal-reference distribution.

evidence.quote: The anomaly-free BTCV set, consisting of 50 abdominal 3D CT scans, constitutes the training set, while the test data comprises 131 abdominal 3D CT scans from LiTS.

all.suggested_fix: Add patient-disjoint, within-LiTS training and testing alongside BTCV-to-LiTS transfer, using equal normal-image and annotation budgets.
all.verdict_reason: BTCV training, LiTS testing, and the missing source-matched control support a possible source confound, but acquisition/population shifts and their contribution to baseline weakness are not demonstrated.

all.limitation: The pixel-wise alignment objective is incompletely specified for OCT17, ChestXray, and HIS, which provide only classification labels.
all.explanation: The training formulation assigns every sample a segmentation mask and optimizes Dice/Focal alignment, yet three datasets are explicitly classification-only. The paper does not explain whether segmentation losses are omitted or masks are derived for these samples, undermining reproducibility and interpretation of the claimed pixel-wise adaptation.

evidence.quote: Each tuple includes a training image $x_i$, its corresponding image-level anomaly classification (AC) label $c_i \in \{-, +\}$, and pixel-level anomaly segmentation (AS) annotations $\mathcal{S}_i\in \{-, +\}^{h\times w}$ for images of size $h\times w$.
Among these, BrainMRI~, LiverCT~, and RESC~ datasets are used for both anomaly classification (AC) and segmentation (AS), while OCT17~, ChestXray~, and HIS~ are solely for AC.

all.suggested_fix: Specify a mask-availability indicator that disables segmentation losses for image-only samples, and ablate their inclusion in cross-domain training.
all.verdict_reason: The formal objective requires Dice/Focal mask supervision, but the paper gives no rule for handling those losses on its three classification-only datasets.

all.limitation: The random K-shot sampling protocol does not specify normal/anomalous quotas despite requiring normal target images to construct the memory bank.
all.explanation: Training samples are described as random labeled subsets, whereas the few-shot branch requires normal references. Without documented class quotas, some K=2 draws could contain no normal images, while other draws could provide substantially different reference coverage, making the branch's definition and comparisons dependent on unspecified sample composition.

evidence.quote: For the few-shot AD scenario, we select a random subset of labeled training samples, with $K\in \{2,4,8,16\}$, from the labeled training set (designated as ``Train (with labels)'' in Table~).

All the multi-level visual features of a few labeled normal images in $\mathcal{D}_{med}$ contribute to constructing a multi-level feature memory bank $\mathcal{G}$ facilitating the feature comparison.

all.suggested_fix: Use fixed K/2 normal and K/2 anomalous patient-disjoint samples, share identical draws across methods, and report the actual normal-bank size.
all.verdict_reason: Random total K-image sampling is described without class quotas even though the few-shot memory bank requires normal images, leaving support composition and zero-normal draws unspecified.

all.limitation: The few-shot experiments do not report pathology-level holdouts, so they cannot establish detection of unseen disease types after adaptation.
all.explanation: OCT17 contains three anomaly categories, but the K-shot protocol samples from the labeled pool without specifying separation of disease types between adaptation and testing. High AUC can therefore reflect adaptation to familiar disease appearances rather than transfer to novel abnormalities, an issue highlighted in the paper's motivation for few-shot AD.

evidence.quote: In contrast, the OCT17 dataset~ primarily serves for classification tasks, featuring retinal OCT images categorized into three types of anomalies.
The utilization of a few known anomalies during training can present challenges, potentially biasing the model and hindering generalization to unseen anomalies.

all.suggested_fix: Run leave-one-pathology-out OCT17 experiments, adapting on the other anomaly types and normal images while testing the held-out type against normals.
all.verdict_reason: The few-shot protocol reports no disease-category exclusion or pathology-held-out evaluation, so it does not isolate transfer from supported to unseen disease types.

all.limitation: The fixed 240-pixel input and bilinearly upsampled ViT patch maps impose a spatial bottleneck that is not evaluated for small lesions or precise boundaries.
all.explanation: ChestXray and RESC begin at substantially higher resolutions than the model input, so fine diagnostic structures may be discarded before inference. Bilinear interpolation cannot recover missing detail, and combining transformer depths does not demonstrate that the resulting masks preserve small lesions or boundary accuracy.

evidence.quote: We utilize the CLIP with ViT-L/14 architecture, with input images at a resolution of 240.
Here, $BI(\cdot)$ reshapes the anomaly map to $\sqrt{G}\times\sqrt{G}$ and restores it to the original input image resolution using bilinear interpolation, with $G$ representing the grid number.

all.suggested_fix: Compare the current pipeline with higher-resolution or tiled inputs and a spatial decoder, reporting lesion-size-stratified Dice and boundary accuracy.
all.verdict_reason: The model uses 240-pixel inputs and bilinearly upsampled patch-grid scores without a lesion-size-stratified or boundary-resolution evaluation of this spatial bottleneck.

all.limitation: Maximum grid-score pooling makes image-level predictions vulnerable to isolated artifacts without a robustness evaluation of this aggregation choice.
all.explanation: At each level, the highest local anomaly score determines the image-level contribution, allowing one acquisition artifact or irrelevant high-scoring patch to control classification. No alternative pooling or artifact stress test establishes whether this extreme-value aggregation produces stable medical predictions.

evidence.quote: c_{zero} = \frac{1}{4}{\textstyle \sum_{l=1}^4}\max_{G}(softmax(\mathcal{F}_{cls,l} \mathcal{F}_{text}^{T})),

all.suggested_fix: Compare max, top-k, and attention pooling on clean images and paired artifact-corrupted normal images, measuring false positives at a locked threshold.
all.verdict_reason: Maximum pooling lets a high-scoring patch dominate a level's contribution and lacks robustness testing, but artifact-driven instability of final predictions is only hypothesized.

all.limitation: Reliance on two averaged generic normal/abnormal text embeddings is not validated for heterogeneous pathology-specific medical semantics.
all.explanation: The text representation compresses diverse diseases into one binary distinction instead of representing their clinical appearances. Because the starting VLM is trained on natural imagery and no prompt-sensitivity comparison is reported, the generic semantic distinction may not align consistently with all target pathologies or organ contexts.

evidence.quote: At the state level, our strategy involves using straightforward, generic text descriptions for normal and abnormal states, focusing on clarity and avoiding complex details.

By calculating the average of the text features extracted by the text encoder for normal and abnormal states separately, we obtain a text feature represented as $\mathcal{F}_{text} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times d}$, where $d$ is the feature dimension.

all.suggested_fix: Compare generic prompts, medically worded prompts, and source-trained learned prompts under identical supervision and strict modality/pathology holdouts.
all.verdict_reason: Binary prompt averaging and missing prompt-sensitivity studies are evident, but the multiple medical benchmarks provide indirect validation, making the broader semantic nonvalidation claim overstated.

all.limitation: Equal-weight fusion combines softmax scores and cosine distances without demonstrating compatible score scales or calibrated branch contributions.
all.explanation: Softmax scores lie between zero and one, whereas cosine distance can range from zero to two and has a different distribution. Setting both weights to 0.5 therefore does not ensure comparable contributions, and modality-dependent score scales can change fused rankings independently of representation quality.

evidence.quote: Here, $Dist(\cdot, \cdot)$ represents the cosine distance, calculated as $1-cosine(\cdot,\cdot)$.
Here, $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are weighting factors for the zero-shot and few-shot branches, respectively, set to 0.5 by default.

all.suggested_fix: Compare text-only, memory-only, raw fusion, and validation-calibrated fusion on the same K-shot draws, fitting all calibration parameters without test labels.
all.verdict_reason: The stated fusion averages softmax probabilities with raw cosine distances using equal coefficients without reported score normalization, calibration, or fusion-weight validation.

all.limitation: No language-free control establishes that visual-language alignment, rather than ordinary supervised multi-level adaptation, drives the transfer gains.
all.explanation: The reported architectural ablations preserve the visual-language alignment objective. A supervised binary visual head could also learn anomaly separation using Dice, Focal, and BCE losses, so these experiments do not isolate the contribution of linguistic knowledge from adaptation and label supervision.

evidence.quote: For this purpose, we substitute the multi-level feature adapters with distinct multi-level feature projectors, while keeping the parameters and feature alignment loss functions the same.

all.suggested_fix: Train a language-free two-class visual-head baseline with identical adapters, labels, losses, parameter budget, and held-out domain splits.
all.verdict_reason: The relevant MVFA ablations retain visual-language alignment, so no matched language-free control separates linguistic knowledge from supervised multi-level adaptation.

all.limitation: The dismissal of MedCLIP's broad generalization is not based on task-matched adaptation, weakening the positioning of natural-image CLIP against medical VLM pretraining.
all.explanation: MedCLIP is evaluated in the few-normal-shot group, whereas MVFA benefits from labeled anomalies and adapter training. Its ChestXray advantage is also attributed to overlapping pretraining data, so the comparison confounds supervision, adaptation, and pretraining coverage rather than isolating the transfer value of medical pretraining.

evidence.quote: (ii) few-normal-shot methods (CLIP~, MedCLIP~, WinCLIP~), and (iii) few-shot methods (DRA~, BGAD~, and April-GAN~).

While MedCLIP~ shows superior results on ChestXray because it was trained on large-scale overlapping ChestXray data in our medical AD benchmark, it lacks broad generalization capabilities, as evidenced by its performance on other datasets.

all.suggested_fix: Adapt capacity-matched medical and natural-image VLMs with the same supervision and comparison scheme, auditing pretraining overlap before comparing generalization.
all.verdict_reason: MedCLIP is evaluated as a few-normal-shot baseline against anomaly-supervised MVFA, with no matched-adaptation experiment controlling supervision and pretraining coverage.

all.limitation: Segmentation evaluation relies solely on pixel-level AUROC, which does not establish accurate lesion masks or lesion-wise detection performance.
all.explanation: Pixel AUROC measures ranking rather than thresholded overlap, boundary quality, or recovery of individual lesions. With coarse, interpolated score maps, high AUROC can coexist with missed small lesions or poorly delineated masks, so near-ceiling AS values do not establish clinically usable segmentation.

evidence.quote: This metric is a standard in AD evaluation, with separate considerations for image-level AUC in AC and pixel-level AUC in AS.

all.suggested_fix: Report Dice, IoU, boundary distance, and lesion-wise FROC at validation-selected thresholds, stratifying results by lesion size.
all.verdict_reason: Quantitative AS evaluation reports pixel ROC AUC without thresholded overlap, boundary, or lesion-wise metrics, leaving those aspects of segmentation quality unestablished.

all.limitation: Random K-shot evaluations are reported only as point estimates, without draw variability, training-seed variance, confidence intervals, or paired significance tests.
all.explanation: Performance with two to sixteen examples can depend strongly on which patients and abnormalities are sampled, but the paper does not report the number of draws or their variability. Consequently, both large dataset-specific gains and small ablation differences lack reliability estimates, and descriptions of significant superiority cannot be interpreted as statistical evidence.

evidence.quote: For the few-shot AD scenario, we select a random subset of labeled training samples, with $K\in \{2,4,8,16\}$, from the labeled training set (designated as ``Train (with labels)'' in Table~).
In our main focus of out-domain evaluations on the medical AD benchmark, MVFA significantly outperforms competing methods, highlighting its superior generalization capabilities.

all.suggested_fix: Repeat evaluation over multiple shared patient-level K-shot draws and training seeds, reporting paired AUC-difference confidence intervals using patient- or slide-clustered bootstrapping.
all.verdict_reason: The random-support experiments provide point AUCs without documented repeat counts, seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

all.limitation: Averaged ablations obscure substantial dataset-specific negative transfer and leave the practical benefit of four-level ensembling unresolved.
all.explanation: Ensembling improves the strongest individual level's mean AC from 88.84 to 88.97 and AS from 98.62 to 98.67, only 0.13 and 0.05 AUC points. Meanwhile, ChestXray Layer 3 AC falls from 79.75 under single-level training to 58.32 under multi-level training. Average improvements therefore do not establish uniformly beneficial cross-level interaction or justify the additional ensemble cost.
all.suggested_fix: Compare Layer-2-only and ensemble models over identical repeated draws, reporting per-domain paired differences and accuracy–latency trade-offs.
all.verdict_reason: The tables show only 0.13/0.05-point ensemble mean gains and a 21.43-point ChestXray Layer 3 regression, without cost-benefit evidence establishing uniformly advantageous ensembling.

all.limitation: The analysis does not systematically explain failure modes, including the zero-shot BrainMRI segmentation regression relative to April-GAN.
all.explanation: BrainMRI segmentation AUROC is 90.27 for MVFA versus 91.79 for April-GAN, but this regression is not investigated. Although visualizations mark some missed or erroneous regions, selected examples do not quantify errors by lesion size, pathology, or image quality. Without such decomposition, the conditions under which cross-domain adaptation fails remain unclear.

evidence.quote: To qualitatively analyze how the proposed multi-level feature adaptation approach improves anomaly segmentation performance, we visualize the results of several cases from the BrainMRI, LiverCT, and RESC datasets.

all.suggested_fix: Conduct a blinded expert audit of false positives and false negatives, tabulating rates by lesion size, pathology, and acquisition quality for each modality.
all.verdict_reason: The BrainMRI AS deficit appears in the zero-shot table, but selected visualizations are not accompanied by a systematic investigation of the regression or error categories.

all.limitation: Balanced BrainMRI and nearly balanced HIS test sampling, combined with AUROC-only reporting, does not establish clinical operating thresholds or false-positive burden.
all.explanation: Clinical anomaly prevalence and case spectrum can differ substantially from balanced slice or patch samples. AUROC neither selects a usable threshold nor determines positive predictive value, calibration, or false alarms per patient at deployment prevalence, so ranking performance alone cannot establish safe triage.

evidence.quote: The training set encompasses 7,500 normal samples, while the test set comprises 3,715 samples with a balanced ratio of normal to anomaly instances.
For testing, 1,003 normal and 997 abnormal patches from the 115 testing WSIs are utilized.
The area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve metric (AUC) is used to quantify the performance.

all.suggested_fix: Evaluate consecutive clinical cases at observed prevalence using a separately selected, locked threshold, reporting sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, calibration, and false alarms per study.
all.verdict_reason: The balanced slice/patch test sets and ROC-AUC-only results provide no deployment-prevalence precision, calibrated operating threshold, or patient-level false-alarm estimate.
